chapter_theme: Pattiragiriyar's lament opens: every couplet asks 'when?' (எக்காலம்) for a step he has not yet taken. The steps run from burning off the senses and the sleep that is not sleep, through the flood of grace, the cutting of birth's delusion and the taking of the body-fort, to the renunciations: women forgotten, kin seen as false, no life killed, idols seen for what they are, the tortoise's withdrawal, and wandering the world like a corpse before Yama sends him back to the womb.
structure_note: Twenty-four kannis after an unnumbered invocation to the elephant-faced god. The stanzas chain: the second line of one becomes the first of the next (3 and 4 the flood of grace, 5 and 6 birth's delusion, 6 and 7 the fort of the body, 8 and 9 wandering like a ghost), so the lament advances by small turns rather than by topics. Only 17 uses the refrain as sarcasm: the idols will never become the Real.

1.reading: To speak this lament, the word of knowledge that gives release, when shall I receive the grace of the elephant-faced one?
1.nuance: An invocation to Ganapati (அத்திமுகவன், the elephant-faced) outside the work's own numbering; it names the whole poem a புலம்பல் (lament) and claims that its words give release.

2.reading: Burning off the five senses in which the ego hides, and sleeping without sleeping, when shall I gain bliss?
2.nuance: தூங்காமல் தூங்கி, sleeping without sleep, is the yogic stillness that keeps awareness, the state Tirumular calls seeing while asleep. ஆங்காரம் உள்ளடக்கிய can mean the senses that hold the ego within them or the senses the ego has drawn in; either way the ego and the five are burned together. 75 closes the third run with the same verb, சுட்டறுத்து.

3.reading: Staying in the unceasing sleep of Siva-yoga, when shall I dam up the flood of compassion that never dries?
3.nuance: சிவயோக நித்திரை names the sleep of 2 as a yogic state. தேக்குவது (damming, storing) treats grace as water to be held, and 4 then asks to drink it.

4.reading: Having dammed up the flood of compassion in order to drink it, when shall I come and take up the portion I left untaken?
4.nuance: வாங்காமல் விட்ட குறை, the shortfall left unreceived, is taken by tradition as the practice begun in an earlier birth and not finished, which this life is to resume; the plain sense is only 'what I failed to take'. The verse does not say whose the shortfall is.

5.reading: Not broken within and withered by worry that never rests, when shall I cut off the bewilderment of birth that maya brings?
5.nuance: மாயாப் பிறவி can be the birth maya makes or the birth that does not die, that is, keeps returning; the second sense is kept in 6, where the same phrase is cut through.

6.reading: Cutting through the bewilderment of birth that maya brings, when shall I seize the fort of Kayapuri?
6.nuance: காயாபுரிக் கோட்டை is read by tradition as the fort of the body-city (kāya, the body), so that seizing it is mastery of the body in yoga. The spelling காயா also allows 'the city that does not wither'. The verse gives only the name and the act of capture.

7.reading: To bring the fort of Kayapuri under my hand, when shall the direct experience that does not perish come and join me?
7.nuance: மாயா அனுபூதி, undying anubhuti, is direct experience as opposed to learning; it is named as the means to the capture of 6, not its reward. 62 returns to anubhuti as enjoyment (போக அனுபூதி).

8.reading: Becoming like a child, wandering like one deaf and dumb, staying like a ghost, when shall I take on madness for you?
8.nuance: பிரமை is ordinarily delusion; here 'your பிரமை' is the one bewilderment worth having, the mad fixation on the Lord that the Siddhars wear as a guise of idiocy. The child, the deaf-mute and the ghost are the three outward forms of it, and 9 adds the corpse.

9.reading: Wandering like a ghost, lying like a corpse, and thinking of woman as mother, when shall I complete my tapas?
9.nuance: பெண்ணைத் தாய்போல் நினைத்து is the ascetic's standing rule for every woman, and it opens the run of stanzas on women (10 to 13). தவம் முடிப்பது, finishing tapas, recurs in 15 with a different condition.

10.reading: When shall I live forgetting the women who show a foot, show a hand, show the eyes and the face, and so show infatuation?
10.nuance: The four காட்டி set out the woman's display limb by limb, and the fifth, மால்காட்டும், is what the display produces in the one who looks. The verse blames the showing and the forgetting is asked of himself.

11.reading: Leaving off the bewilderment of desire for good women, and closing both eyes, when shall I stay merged?
11.nuance: கண்ணிரண்டும் மூடி, both eyes shut, answers 10's eyes that show: what the eyes are not shown they cannot be caught by. கலந்திருப்பது, staying merged, has no named object; the Lord is understood.

12.reading: When shall I cease being struck and held fast in the pouch of the vulva, spread open like a cut wound?
12.nuance: The image is deliberately ugly: அல்குல் as a wound that has been cut open, and the man as something that has been hit (தட்டுண்டு) and stuck there. 13 keeps the wound and makes it the one that does not heal.

13.reading: Not lying sunk in the wound that does not heal, when shall I console the mind that will not be consoled?
13.nuance: ஆறாத புண் carries over 12's wound and so can be the body of the woman or desire itself; both readings keep the mind as the thing that is stuck. தேறாத சிந்தை, the mind that will not be cleared, is the real subject of the stanza.

14.reading: Seeing in my mind that father, mother, children and brothers are false, when shall I cut off the crookedness within?
14.nuance: பொய் here is not that the kin do not exist but that they are no refuge and no lasting bond, as the Siddhars say of the kin who cannot follow at Death's call. திருக்கு, the twist or crookedness, is the attachment that bends the mind toward them.

15.reading: Not wandering about killing and torturing firm-rooted lives and eating them, but thinking of them as my own life, when shall I complete my tapas?
15.nuance: தன்னுயிர்போல் எண்ணி is the Kural's measure of compassion applied to the renouncer's diet; the stanza names killing, torturing and eating as one act. மன்னுயிர், the lives that abide, is also the Kural's word for living beings.

16.reading: Without earning the name of sinner and falling into the barren hell, when shall I now know the thread that is the breath of life?
16.nuance: ஆவி என்ற சூத்திரம், the sutra of the life-breath, is taken by tradition as the secret working of prana, the Siddhars' breath practice; சூத்திரம் is also the puppet-string and the formula, and the word returns in 39 and 40 with both senses in play. The plain sense, the secret of what the breath is, holds without the practice.

17.reading: A chiselled stone, red paste pressed into a shape, and copper scoured with tamarind: when will these become the Real?
17.nuance: The only stanza where எக்காலம் means never. The three are the materials of images, stone, paste and polished metal, and the verse does not say the god is elsewhere, only that these are not it. பொருள் is the Real, or the thing of value.

18.reading: Amusements, comforts, true display and false display: when shall I live having forgotten the whole habit of them?
18.nuance: மெய்ப்பகட்டும் பொய்ப்பகட்டும் treats show that has something behind it and show that has nothing as one habit (வாடிக்கை) to be dropped; the verse does not rank them.

19.reading: Leaving behind silk clothes, gold ornaments, pretence and evil deeds, when shall I desire your feet?
19.nuance: பாவனை, pretence or imagining, sits between the ornaments and the deeds: the finery, the self-image and the sins are one list. The first address to 'you' (உன்பாதம்) in the poem.

20.reading: Like a tortoise that sees a man coming and draws in its five, when shall I take the form of a mute and subside?
20.nuance: The Kural's tortoise, with the man approaching added: the withdrawal is from a seen danger. ஊமை உரு, the shape of a mute, joins the deaf-mute of 8 to the drawn-in senses, so that silence is the restraint's outward sign.

21.reading: Palanquins, halting-houses, latticed windows and mansions: when shall the thought that delights in the sight of them cease?
21.nuance: The four are things seen, not owned; கண்டு களிக்கும் கருத்து, the mind that enjoys looking, is the fault, which is why the stanza follows the silk and gold of 19.

22.reading: Having searched out and seen the Father's dwelling-place, when shall I now wander daily like a dead corpse?
22.nuance: The order matters: first the place where the Father is, found by inquiry (ஆராய்ந்து), and only then the corpse-like wandering of 9 and 23. The place is not named; the Siddhars put it within the body or the heart.

23.reading: Keeping what remains of dharma, and seeing the bones within as white bones, when shall I now see myself lowered like a cast-off corpse?
23.nuance: ஒழிந்த தருமம் may be the dharma that remains after renunciation, or the dharma one has given up; the syntax does not settle it. The second line is corrupt in the source (போல்இ ழிந்து for போல் இழிந்து). The sense that holds is seeing one's own body already as the skeleton it will be.

24.reading: Forgetting petty pleasure, knowing awareness by awareness, when shall I cut off the hold that falling into the womb has taken on me?
24.nuance: அறிவை அறிவால் அறிந்து, knowing awareness by awareness itself, is the knowledge the Siddhars set above books. கோள் is a hold or seizure, and also a planet: the grip rebirth took on him, or the planetary fate fixed at conception; the first fits the chain into 25.

25.reading: Before Yama takes me by the hand and puts me back into a womb, when shall I agree to be shaped and ruled by you?
25.nuance: The pair கருப்படுத்தி (putting into the womb) and உருப்படுத்தி (giving form, setting right) makes Yama and the Lord rivals for the same work on the same body. The run ends on உடன்படுவது, consent, as the one thing asked of himself.

links.note: Both make a sleep that is not sleep the state of yoga: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will sleep without sleeping (தூங்காமல் தூங்கி) and gain bliss; Tirumular says those who slept saw Siva's world, yoga and enjoyment within themselves (தூங்கிக் கண்டார்). 3 names the same state சிவயோக நித்திரை.

The Kural asks why one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு) does hurtful things to other lives (மன்னுயிர்க்கு); Pattiragiriyar uses the same two words and asks when he will stop killing and eating மன்னுயிர் and think of them தன்னுயிர்போல். The Kural's rule of compassion becomes a condition of finishing tapas.

Tirumular's first mark of one who stands in yama is கொல்லான், he does not kill, before truth, restraint and freedom from drink and lust; Pattiragiriyar makes not killing and eating lives the condition of completing tapas. In both the yogic path begins in the ethics of harm.

Sivavakkiyar lists brick, black stone, the red jati lingam, copper and brass as the things people say Siva dwells in, and asks whether the dance in the hall can be found there; Pattiragiriyar asks when chiselled stone, shaped red paste and tamarind-scoured copper will become the Real. The materials of the image are the same and the answer in both is never.

The Kural's tortoise draws in its five in one birth and is protected for seven; Pattiragiriyar's tortoise draws in its five on seeing a man come (ஆள்கண்டு), and he asks when he will do likewise and subside as a mute. Pattiragiriyar adds the approaching danger and takes the withdrawal into silence rather than into future births.

Tirumular says the five draw in like a tortoise's limbs when the silent letter meets the spoken, and the result is beyond names; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will draw in like the tortoise and take the shape of a mute (ஊமை உரு). Both carry the Kural's image past restraint into silence.

Pattiragiriyar asks to search out and see the Father's dwelling-place (அத்தன் இருப்பிடம்) and then go through the world as a corpse; Tirumular says he is not in the mansion, hall, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing. 2614 gives the answer 22 goes looking for, and both put it inside rather than in any building or dress.

In both Death is the one who puts a person into the womb: Tirumular's harsh Kalan sets the base in the womb-pit (கருக்குழி) and they fall in again; Pattiragiriyar's Yama takes him by the hand and makes him an embryo (கருப்படுத்தி). Pattiragiriyar adds the rival act, the Lord shaping him (உருப்படுத்தி), before that happens.

Tirumular: before Death comes in force, which does not ask who you are, do good tapas; Pattiragiriyar: before Yama takes his hand and sends him to a womb, consent to be ruled. Both make the time before Death's arrival the only time there is, and both ask for an act of the will now.

23: போல்இ ழிந்து is a broken word division for போல் இழிந்து.
